paras: The attempted lynching of John Jackson took place at Zwolle, Louisiana, in August 1903, when a Black man accused of assaulting the wife of a local man was nearly lynched after his capture. A constable got Jackson to the parish prison, and the story ran in the New York Sun under the headline "Negro Saved From Lynching."

Zwolle was described as "a small town on the Kansas City Southern Railroad". According to a New Orleans dispatch dated August 21, Jackson was accused of assaulting the wife of Harry Mason there, and Mrs. Mason was said to have been badly injured "in her struggle with the negro."

Jackson was captured shortly after the alleged assault, taken before Mrs. Mason, and identified by her. The dispatch then says that "an attempt was made to lynch him at Zwolle," though its opening sentence places the near-lynching "near Many, Sabine Point, La." The would-be lynchers are not described or counted, and the constable "succeeded in getting him to the parish prison."
No report of an indictment, trial or later outcome for Jackson was found, and no arrests of those who tried to lynch him were reported.

The only coverage found is the New Orleans wire item the New York Sun printed on page 7 on August 22, 1903. Under the headline "Negro Saved From Lynching," it told the accusation as fact, called Jackson "a negro" and "the negro," and framed the constable's action as a rescue. No Louisiana paper and no Black newspaper was found to have reported the case.

bases: The only report describes an attempt to lynch an accused Black man that failed when a constable got him to the parish prison (A1).
Jackson was 'nearly lynched' but reached the parish prison alive, so no one was killed; the would-be lynchers are not described or counted, though the attempt followed an accusation of assault (A1).
Only one wire dispatch, printed in the New York Sun, was found; no local, other white or Black-press report turned up (A1).

accounts.label: Wire report (New Orleans dispatch)
accounts.gist: Jackson assaulted Mrs. Mason, was captured and identified by her, and narrowly escaped lynching when the constable got him to the parish prison; the assault is presented as fact.

framing.detail: The Sun ran the New Orleans dispatch on page 7 under 'Negro Saved From Lynching', calling Jackson 'the negro' and treating the accusation as established.

record_check.dossier: He had been captured and the attempt was made on a prisoner, but he was not taken: the constable got him to the parish prison
1903-08-21 is the dispatch date; the events occurred on or before it
The dispatch prints 'Sabine Point, La.' and names no parish; Sabine is a reading of that phrase
Capture, identification before the accuser, and a failed lynching attempt

info: On or before August 21, 1903 (date of the New Orleans dispatch; the day of the assault and attempt is not given)
Assault alleged at Zwolle, 'a small town on the Kansas City Southern Railroad'; Jackson 'nearly lynched near Many, Sabine Point [as printed], La.'; the lynching attempt placed at Zwolle
Accused of assault on the wife of Harry Mason at Zwolle; the dispatch says Mrs. Mason was badly injured in the struggle
Not described; the dispatch says only that 'an attempt was made to lynch him'
Jackson was lodged in the parish prison; no later report of a trial or other outcome was found

sources.note: New Orleans, Aug. 21 dispatch 'Negro Saved From Lynching': Jackson accused of assaulting Mrs. Harry Mason at Zwolle, nearly lynched, constable got him to the parish prison; the only report found.
quotes: John Jackson, a negro, was nearly lynched near Many, Sabine Point, La., for assault on the wife of Harry Mason at Zwolle
